title: The Rise of Open Models in the Enterprise — Amir Haghighat, Baseten

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's core subject is production inference serving complexity—speculative decoding, prefix caching, disaggregated serving, framework reliability, and autoscaling. The speaker explicitly advocates horizontal AI tooling across diverse industries and pitches Baseten as a developer platform for inference infrastructure. The discussion centers on enterprises running models in production and the scaling challenges that emerge when adopting open models. Requires familiarity with inference serving frameworks, speculative decoding techniques, and GPU-based deployment concepts. A single-speaker conference presentation at the AI Engineer conference. Claims are grounded in 100+ enterprise conversations with quantitative examples, though the speaker is a vendor with an acknowledged commercial bias.

summary: Amir Haghighat, co-founder and CTO of Baseten, shares patterns from 100+ enterprise conversations about AI adoption. He frames enterprise adoption as critical to AI's ultimate impact given enterprises' scale and budget. He sells horizontal AI tooling and argues true value unlocks when enterprises build with AI themselves, not just buy verticalized solutions—analogizing to how Snowflake and Datadog emerged. The enterprise journey begins with OpenAI and Anthropic via dedicated deployments on Azure or AWS. Over time attitudes shifted: 2023 was dismissive, 2024 saw 40-50 of ~100 enterprises with production use cases, and 2025 shows palpable cracks in the assumption that closed frontier models suffice indefinitely. The cracks are not vendor lock-in (multiple interoperable providers exist), ballooning per-token cost (prices are plummeting), or compliance/security (CSPs handle these). The real cracks are: quality for specific tasks (medical document extraction and transcription outperforming generic APIs with labeled data), latency (frontier APIs optimize throughput not latency, critical for AI voice), unit economics (agentic use cases can trigger 50 inference calls per user action, breaking per-token pricing), and 'destiny' (CIOs/CTOs questioning competitive alpha if everyone uses the same frontier models). Adopting open models forces enterprises to build inference infrastructure far more complex than combining a model, serving framework (vLLM, SGLang, TRT-LLM), and GPUs. Amir details 'dragons' at the performance layer: speculative decoding technique selection (draft models, Medusa heads, Eagle 3, MTP) requires staying on top of fast-moving research, and optimizations bleed from model level to infrastructure level—prefix caching and disaggregated serving matter greatly for agentic use cases with massive but similar prompts, affecting time-to-first-token and P99 reliability. Mission-critical inference requires four nines, but the naive formula yields only ~two nines; vLLM and Triton crash often, and hardware failures cause tail latency spikes. Autoscaling is slow—one enterprise reports eight minutes to bring up a new replica. Additional dragons include tooling lifecycle management, observability (a 'massive iceberg'), controls, and audits. These challenges culminate in a build-or-buy decision, where Amir pitches Baseten as the buy option. He closes by inviting conversations with enterprises and startups at Baseten's booth and happy hour.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Enterprise AI adoption is the true signal of whether AI is hype or real, given enterprises' scale and budget.
Enterprises start with closed models (OpenAI, Anthropic) on dedicated cloud deployments but cracks appeared palpably in 2025.
Real drivers toward open source: task-specific quality, latency sensitivity, ballooning agentic inference costs, and competitive differentiation—not vendor lock-in, per-token cost, or compliance.
Production inference is far more complex than model + serving framework + GPUs; significant hidden infrastructure 'dragons' exist.
Speculative decoding technique selection (draft models, Medusa, Eagle 3, MTP) requires ongoing research tracking and is not a simple switch flip.
The naive model-plus-framework-plus-GPU formula yields only ~two nines of reliability, not the four nines mission-critical inference demands.
Serving framework crashes (vLLM, Triton) and slow autoscaling (e.g., 8-minute replica spin-up) cause severe tail latency spikes.
Observability, tooling lifecycle management, controls, and audits are additional dragons enterprises must address.
The cumulative infrastructure complexity forces a build-or-buy decision, which is Baseten's core pitch.
Understand the enterprise AI adoption journey from closed to open models and the timeline of changing attitudes.

sections.title: Introduction and Why Enterprise AI Adoption Matters
sections.summary: Amir introduces himself as Baseten co-founder/CTO and frames the talk around enterprise AI adoption. He argues enterprise adoption is the key indicator of whether AI is hype or real, since enterprises have massive reach and budget, and slow adoption would mean a slow paradigm shift.

sections.title: Speaker's Background and Horizontal vs. Vertical AI Tooling
sections.summary: Amir explains his vantage point from 100+ enterprise conversations over two years, spanning public software companies to Fortune 50 consumer companies. He highlights his bias toward horizontal tooling and argues true value unlocks when enterprises build with AI, not just buy verticalized products, drawing an analogy to Snowflake and Datadog.

sections.title: The Enterprise Journey with Closed Models
sections.summary: Enterprises start with OpenAI and Anthropic on dedicated Azure/AWS deployments for security and privacy. Amir traces the timeline: 2023 was dismissive, 2024 saw 40-50 of ~100 enterprises with production use cases, and 2025 shows palpable cracks in the assumption that closed models suffice indefinitely.

sections.title: What the Cracks Are Not
sections.summary: Amir dispels misconceptions: vendor lock-in is not a concern (multiple interoperable providers), ballooning per-token cost is not an issue (prices are plummeting), and compliance/privacy/security are handled by CSPs running models inside enterprise VPCs.

sections.title: The Real Cracks: Quality, Latency, Unit Economics, Destiny
sections.summary: The real drivers toward open models are: quality for specific tasks (medical document extraction, medical transcription outperforming generic APIs), latency (frontier APIs optimize throughput not latency, critical for AI voice), unit economics (agentic use cases can trigger 50 inference calls per user action, breaking per-token economics), and 'destiny' (competitive differentiation through owning AI capabilities).

sections.title: The Inference Infrastructure Challenge ('Dragons')
sections.summary: Moving to open models means building inference infrastructure. Amir warns the common assumption—model + vLLM/SGLang/TRT-LLM + GPUs equals production inference—is false. He begins detailing 'dragons,' starting with the performance layer: latency optimization requires coordinated work at both the model level (e.g., speculative decoding) and the infrastructure level.

sections.title: Dragons Continued: Speculative Decoding, Reliability, Scaling, and Build-vs-Buy
sections.summary: Amir elaborates on speculative decoding technique choices (draft models, Medusa heads, Eagle 3, MTP) requiring ongoing research tracking. Optimizations bleed into infrastructure: prefix caching and disaggregated serving are critical for agentic use cases with massive but similar prompts, affecting time-to-first-token and P99. The naive formula yields only ~two nines, not four; vLLM and Triton crash often, causing tail latency spikes. Autoscaling is slow—one enterprise reports 8-minute replica spin-ups. Additional dragons include tooling lifecycle management, observability (a 'massive iceberg'), controls, and audits. These challenges culminate in a build-or-buy decision, Amir's pitch for Baseten. He closes by inviting enterprise and startup conversations at Baseten's booth and a happy hour.

demonstrations: Health plans building custom medical document extraction (CPT codes, diagnosis codes, prescriptions) that outperforms generic Claude/GPT using their accumulated labeled data.
Healthcare voice transcription models fine-tuned to understand medical jargon better than generic API-based models.
Soft drink company reporting 8-minute spin-up time for a new model replica, illustrating slow autoscaling challenges.
limitations: Speaker acknowledges a bias: he sells horizontal AI tooling, so his perspective emphasizes building over buying verticalized solutions.
Observations are based on conversations with enterprises that engage with Baseten, potentially a self-selected sample.
The 'destiny' rationale for open model adoption is described as 'a bit vibby' and emerging only recently.
The build-or-buy framing naturally biases toward Baseten's commercial offering.
quantitativeClaims: 100+ enterprises consulted over the past two years.
In 2024, roughly 40-50 out of ~100 enterprises had something in production.
Agentic use cases can result in up to 50 inference calls per single user action.
Baseten is six years old; concentrated enterprise engagement has been over the past two years.
Eagle 3 speculative decoding paper came out approximately six months ago and is already running in production.
The naive model + framework + GPU formula yields only about two nines of reliability, not four nines.
One enterprise reported 8 minutes to bring up a new replica of the same model.
